{"AIM-MATH/ch1/s1": {"body": "

Vectors and Matrices

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, like a single data point with several features. A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers: a whole dataset stacked row by row, or the weights of a neural network layer.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a vector as one customer described by [age, income, visits], and a matrix as a spreadsheet where every row is a customer and every column is a feature.

The Dot Product

The dot product multiplies matching entries and sums them, measuring how much two vectors point the same way. For a=[1,2,3], b=[4,5,6]: 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

To multiply A (m×n) by B (n×p), each output entry (i,j) is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. The result is m×p; the inner dimensions n must match.

Worked Example

A = [[1, 2],      B = 5634           [7, 8]]
AB[0][0] = 1*5 + 2*7 = 19
AB[0][1] = 1*6 + 2*8 = 22
AB[1][0] = 3*5 + 4*7 = 43
AB[1][1] = 3*6 + 4*8 = 50
AB = 19224350
📝 KEY IDEA

A neural network layer computes y = Wx + b: a matrix-vector product plus a bias. Stacking layers just chains matrix multiplications with nonlinearities between them.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: AB ≠ BA in general, and BA may not even be defined if shapes do not line up.

📊 FIGURE — two facts that get asked directly
🎯 EXAM TIP
AI = IA = A — the identity is the matrix version of multiplying by 1, and it is the one matrix that commutes with everything. And transposing a 3×2 gives a 2×3: the shape flips. Watch the order reversal in (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ, which is where marks usually go.
"}, "AIM-MATH/ch1/s2": {"body": "

Vector Spaces and Linear Combinations

A linear combination scales each vector and adds them: c1*v1 + c2*v2 + .... The set of ALL such combinations is their span.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If two vectors point in different directions on a table, mixing them in every ratio reaches any point on the tabletop. That flat surface is their span.

Independence and Basis

Vectors are linearly independent if none can be built from the others. A basis is a minimal independent set that spans the whole space. Its size is the dimension.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Test independence by setting a linear combination to zero. If only all-zero coefficients work, they are independent; a nonzero solution means one vector is redundant.

Worked Example

Are [1,0], [0,1], [2,3] independent? In 2D at most 2 vectors can be independent, so the third is redundant: [2,3] = 2*[1,0] + 3*[0,1]. They span the plane but are NOT independent.

📝 KEY IDEA

The rank of a matrix is its number of linearly independent columns (equal to independent rows). It reveals the true dimensionality of the information it carries.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Many vectors does not mean high dimension. Ten copies of one direction still span only a 1D line; redundancy inflates count but not rank.

📊 FIGURE — how large a rank can be
🎯 EXAM TIP
The largest possible rank of a 5×3 matrix is 3, because rank cannot exceed min(rows, columns). The reason it is min and not something subtler is the theorem that row rank always equals column rank — so the smaller dimension is the binding constraint.
"}, "AIM-MATH/ch1/s3": {"body": "

Special Directions

An eigenvector of A is a nonzero vector v whose direction is unchanged under A: Av = λv. The scalar λ is the eigenvalue, the amount v is stretched or shrunk.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Most vectors get rotated by a matrix. Eigenvectors are the stubborn ones that only get longer or shorter, keeping their line, like the axes a spinning object turns around.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Solve det(A − λI) = 0, the characteristic equation, for the eigenvalues. For each λ, solve (A − λI)v = 0 to find its eigenvectors.

Worked Example

A = 2003
det(A - λI) = (2-λ)(3-λ) = 0
Eigenvalues: λ = 2 and λ = 3
Eigenvector for λ=2: [1, 0]
Eigenvector for λ=3: [0, 1]
📝 KEY IDEA

For a covariance matrix, eigenvectors are the directions of greatest variance and eigenvalues are the variance amounts. This is exactly what PCA finds.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The zero vector is never an eigenvector. Eigenvectors must be nonzero; only their direction matters, so any nonzero scaling of one is also valid.

📊 FIGURE — solving det(A − λI) = 0
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Working the characteristic equation

For A = [[5, 2], [2, 5]]:

det(A − λI) = (5 − λ)(5 − λ) − (2)(2) = (5 − λ)² − 4 = 0

So (5 − λ)² = 4, giving 5 − λ = ±2 and therefore λ = 3 and λ = 7.

Two sanity checks worth doing every time:

  • Trace = sum of eigenvalues: 5 + 5 = 10 = 7 + 3 ✓
  • Determinant = product: 25 − 4 = 21 = 7 × 3 ✓

The eigenvectors are [1, 1] for λ = 7 and [1, −1] for λ = 3 — orthogonal, which is guaranteed for any symmetric matrix.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Check eigenvalues against the trace (their sum) and the determinant (their product) before committing — for [[5,2],[2,5]] that is 10 and 21, satisfied by 7 and 3. It catches sign slips in seconds. Symmetric matrices additionally guarantee real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
"}, "AIM-MATH/ch1/s4": {"body": "

Orthogonality

Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, meeting at a right angle. A set is orthonormal if mutually orthogonal and each of length 1.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Projecting a vector onto a line is the shadow it casts straight down onto that line under a noon sun: the closest point on the line to the original.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The projection of b onto a is (a·b / a·a) a. The leftover b − proj is orthogonal to a: the error you cannot capture along a.

Least Squares

When Ax = b has no exact solution, we minimize squared error. The solution satisfies the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b, projecting b onto A's column space.

Worked Example

Project b=[2,2] onto a=[1,0]:
a·b = 2*1 + 2*0 = 2,  a·a = 1
proj = (2/1)*[1,0] = [2,0]
error = b - proj = [0,2]  (orthogonal to a)
📝 KEY IDEA

Linear regression IS least squares: it projects the target onto the space spanned by the feature columns, minimizing squared residuals.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Least squares minimizes the SUM OF SQUARED errors, not absolute errors, which is why it is sensitive to outliers.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch1/s5": {"body": "

Singular Value Decomposition

Any matrix A factors as A = U Σ V^T. U and V are orthogonal (rotations/reflections) and Σ is diagonal with nonnegative singular values ordered largest to smallest.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

SVD says every linear transformation is really: rotate, stretch along axes, rotate again. The singular values are the stretch amounts.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

PCA centers the data, then finds the top directions of variance: the top right-singular vectors of the data matrix (equivalently, eigenvectors of the covariance matrix). Projecting onto the first k reduces dimensions while keeping most variance.

Worked Example

Suppose singular values are 5, 4, 1. Total energy is 5^2+4^2+1^2 = 42. Keeping the top two captures (25+16)/42 ≈ 98% of variance, so dropping the third loses ~2%.

📝 KEY IDEA

Truncating SVD to the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation of a matrix, the foundation of image compression, recommenders, and PCA.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

PCA is scale-sensitive: features on larger numeric scales dominate variance. Standardize first, or the largest-unit feature hijacks the top components.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch2/s1": {"body": "

What a Derivative Measures

The derivative of f at a point is the slope of the tangent line: how fast the output changes as the input nudges. We write f'(x) or df/dx.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If f(x) is your position over time, f'(x) is your speedometer reading at that instant, the rate right now, not the average over the whole trip.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Power rule: d/dx[x^n] = n·x^(n-1). Chain rule: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) · g'(x). You multiply the outer rate by the inner rate.

Worked Example

f(x) = (3x + 1)^2
Let g = 3x+1, so f = g^2
f'(x) = 2g * g' = 2(3x+1) * 3 = 6(3x+1)
At x=1: f'(1) = 6*4 = 24
📝 KEY IDEA

Deep networks are deeply nested functions. Training uses the chain rule to multiply local derivatives layer by layer; that chained product is exactly backpropagation.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Forgetting the inner derivative. d/dx[sin(2x)] is 2cos(2x), NOT cos(2x): the factor of 2 from inside is required by the chain rule.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch2/s2": {"body": "

Partial Derivatives

When a function has several inputs, a partial derivative measures its rate of change with respect to ONE variable while holding the others fixed. We write ∂f/∂x.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

On a hillside, the partial in the east direction is how steep the ground is if you walk only east. The gradient combines all such slopes into one arrow pointing straight uphill.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The gradient ∇f is the vector of all partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest ascent, and its magnitude is how steep that ascent is.

Worked Example

f(x, y) = x^2 + 3xy
∂f/∂x = 2x + 3y   (treat y as constant)
∂f/∂y = 3x        (treat x as constant)
Gradient at (1, 2): ∇f = [2+6, 3] = [8, 3]
📝 KEY IDEA

To minimize a loss we step in the direction of the NEGATIVE gradient, steepest descent, because that reduces the function fastest.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The gradient points uphill (ascent), not downhill. Gradient descent must negate it. A zero gradient marks a critical point but not necessarily a minimum.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch2/s3": {"body": "

Finding and Classifying Extrema

To optimize a multivariable function, first find critical points where the gradient is zero, then classify each using curvature from the Hessian, the matrix of second partial derivatives.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A critical point is anywhere the ground is flat: the bottom of a valley (min), the top of a hill (max), or a mountain pass (saddle) that goes up one way and down another.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

At a critical point, a positive-definite Hessian (all eigenvalues > 0) means a local minimum; all eigenvalues < 0 means a maximum; mixed signs mean a saddle point.

Worked Example

f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2
∇f = [2x, 2y] = 0  at  (0,0)
Hessian = 2002, eigenvalues 2,2 > 0
=> (0,0) is a local (and global) minimum
📝 KEY IDEA

In high-dimensional network loss surfaces, saddle points, not bad local minima, are the dominant obstacle that slows gradient descent.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A zero gradient alone does NOT confirm a minimum. Without checking curvature you might be at a maximum or a saddle where training stalls.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch2/s4": {"body": "

Learning by Gradients

Training a network means adjusting weights to reduce a loss. The forward pass computes predictions and loss; the backward pass (backpropagation) computes how the loss changes with each weight.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Backprop is like assigning blame. After a wrong answer it works backward asking each weight, 'how much did you contribute to the error?' and nudges it accordingly.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Backprop applies the chain rule from the loss backward, reusing each layer's local gradient. Each weight updates by w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w, where η is the learning rate.

Worked Example

Loss L = (y_pred - y)^2,  y_pred = w*x
∂L/∂y_pred = 2(y_pred - y)
∂y_pred/∂w = x
∂L/∂w = 2(y_pred - y) * x   (chain rule)
Update: w ← w - η * ∂L/∂w
📝 KEY IDEA

Backprop is an efficient, ordered application of the chain rule that reuses intermediate results, so gradients for millions of parameters cost about one extra forward pass.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A learning rate too large makes updates overshoot and diverge; too small makes training crawl. It scales the gradient step and must be tuned.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch3/s1": {"body": "

Random Variables and Distributions

A random variable takes values with certain probabilities. A distribution assigns those probabilities. Discrete variables (a die roll) use a probability mass function; continuous ones (a height) use a density.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Expectation is the long-run average if you repeated the experiment forever. Variance measures how spread out outcomes are around that average: small means predictable, large means erratic.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Expectation: E[X] = Σ x·P(x). Variance: Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])^2] = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2. The standard deviation is its square root.

Worked Example

Fair die: values 1..6 each prob 1/6
E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5
E[X^2] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.17
Var(X) = 15.17 - 3.5^2 = 15.17 - 12.25 ≈ 2.92
📝 KEY IDEA

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is central to ML: noise models, weight initializations, and the Central Limit Theorem all rely on it.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Variance is in squared units. To compare spread on the original scale, use the standard deviation, not the variance itself.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch3/s2": {"body": "

Updating Beliefs

Bayes' theorem revises a probability given evidence: P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E). The prior P(H) is belief before evidence; the likelihood P(E|H) is how well H explains the evidence; the posterior P(H|E) is the updated belief.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

You start with a hunch (prior). Evidence arrives. Bayes tells you exactly how much to shift it: strong evidence moves it a lot, weak evidence barely at all.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Multiply prior by likelihood, then normalize by the total probability of the evidence. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) instead picks parameters that make the observed data most probable.

Worked Example

Disease affects 1% (prior). Test 90% sensitive,
8% false positive.
P(pos)=0.9*0.01 + 0.08*0.99 = 0.009+0.0792=0.0882
P(disease|pos)=0.009/0.0882 ≈ 0.102 (~10%)

Even a positive test leaves only ~10% chance of disease, because it is rare.

📝 KEY IDEA

Training many ML models is MLE (or MAP): minimizing cross-entropy loss is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the training labels.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The base-rate fallacy: ignoring the prior. A positive test on a rare condition can still mean low probability, as the example shows.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch3/s3": {"body": "

Memoryless Processes

A Markov chain models a system moving among states where the next state depends ONLY on the current state, not the full history. This is the Markov property.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Tomorrow's weather depends on today's, not last week's. A Markov chain forgets the past beyond the present state; the present holds all the information you need.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A transition matrix P holds probabilities P[i][j] of moving from state i to state j; each row sums to 1. From distribution x, one step gives xP, and n steps give xP^n.

Worked Example

States Sunny/Rainy. P = 0.80.20.40.6
Start Sunny x=[1,0].
After one step: xP = [0.8, 0.2]
After two steps: [0.8,0.2]P = [0.72, 0.28]
📝 KEY IDEA

Many chains converge to a stationary distribution π satisfying πP = π. PageRank, MCMC sampling, and reinforcement learning all rest on Markov dynamics.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

In the row-vector convention, rows (not columns) of the transition matrix must sum to 1. Mixing up the convention flips which dimension normalizes.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch3/s4": {"body": "

Testing Claims with Data

Hypothesis testing asks whether observed data is surprising under a default assumption, the null hypothesis (H0). The alternative (H1) is what we suspect instead.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

It works like a courtroom: the null hypothesis is innocent by default. We only convict (reject H0) if the evidence would be very unlikely for an innocent defendant.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true. If p is below a threshold α (often 0.05) we reject H0. A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values.

Worked Example

New model beats old by 3% accuracy.
H0: no real difference. Test yields p = 0.02.
Since 0.02 < 0.05, reject H0:
the improvement is statistically significant.
📝 KEY IDEA

Reporting uncertainty (confidence intervals, error bars) on model metrics matters as much as the point estimate: a 1% gain within noise is not real progress.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A p-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true, and a non-significant result does not prove H0. Testing many hypotheses inflates false positives.

📊 FIGURE — why 10 tests at 0.05 is not a 5% risk
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The 40% you did not sign up for

Each independent test at α = 0.05 has a 95% chance of not producing a false positive. Across ten of them:

P(no false positive) = 0.95¹⁰ = 0.5987

P(at least one) = 1 − 0.5987 = 0.4013 ≈ 40%

So running ten tests at the usual threshold gives roughly a two-in-five chance of a spurious "significant" result.

Bonferroni divides the family-wise rate by the number of tests:

0.05 / 10 = 0.005

It is conservative — it protects the family-wise rate at the cost of power. When you are screening hundreds of hypotheses and can tolerate some false discoveries, Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate instead and keeps more power.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The Bonferroni-corrected threshold for 10 tests at a family-wise rate of 0.05 is 0.005 — divide α by the number of tests. Know the motivating number too: ten uncorrected tests carry about a 40% chance of at least one false positive, which is the reason the correction exists.
"}, "AIM-MATH/ch4/s1": {"body": "

Descending the Loss

Gradient descent minimizes a loss by stepping opposite the gradient: θ ← θ − η·∇L(θ). The learning rate η controls step size.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine hiking downhill in fog. You feel the slope underfoot and step downhill. The learning rate is your stride: too long and you overshoot the valley, too short and you barely move.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Batch GD uses the full dataset per step (accurate but slow). Stochastic GD (SGD) uses one example (noisy but fast). Mini-batch GD uses a small batch, balancing stability and speed, the deep learning standard.

Worked Example

Minimize L(θ)=θ^2. ∇L = 2θ. η=0.1, start θ=5.
Step1: θ = 5 - 0.1*10 = 4
Step2: θ = 4 - 0.1*8  = 3.2
Step3: θ = 3.2 - 0.1*6.4 = 2.56 ...  → 0
📝 KEY IDEA

SGD's noise is a feature: it helps escape shallow saddle points and lets training process massive datasets one small batch at a time.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Too large a learning rate can make the loss oscillate or diverge; too small wastes compute. Learning-rate tuning or schedules are essential.

📊 FIGURE — the vocabulary of a training loop
🎯 EXAM TIP
With 10,000 examples and a mini-batch of 100 there are 100 parameter updates in one epoch — steps per epoch is simply N ÷ batch size. The relationship worth carrying: halving the batch size doubles the number of updates per epoch, which is why batch size and learning rate are usually tuned together.
"}, "AIM-MATH/ch4/s2": {"body": "

Why Convexity Matters

A function is convex if the segment between any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph. Equivalently it curves upward everywhere (non-negative second derivative).

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A convex loss is a single smooth bowl. Drop a marble anywhere and it rolls to the one lowest point. A non-convex loss is a bumpy landscape with many dips to get stuck in.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

For a convex function, any local minimum is automatically the global minimum, and gradient descent converges to it with a suitable step size. A set is convex if it contains the segment between any two of its points.

Worked Example

f(x) = x^2 is convex: f''(x) = 2 ≥ 0 everywhere.
Check midpoint of x=-2 and x=2:
f(-2)=4, f(2)=4, average = 4
f(0) = 0 ≤ 4  (graph lies below the chord)
📝 KEY IDEA

Linear and logistic regression with standard losses are convex, so they have unique solutions. Deep networks are non-convex, which is why initialization and optimizer choice matter.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Convexity rules out bad local minima but does NOT guarantee fast convergence: a poorly conditioned convex problem can still be slow without scaling or preconditioning.

📊 FIGURE — what you can do to convex functions
🎯 EXAM TIP
Of the usual options, max(f, g) is the one guaranteed convex — its epigraph is the intersection of two convex epigraphs, and intersections of convex sets are convex. Minimum, difference and product can all fail. This is why hinge loss (a max) and sums of convex losses stay convex, keeping the optimisation well behaved.
"}, "AIM-MATH/ch4/s3": {"body": "

Penalizing Complexity

Regularization adds a penalty on large weights to the loss, discouraging overly complex models that memorize noise. This improves generalization to new data.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Regularization is a simplicity tax. The model can still fit the data, but it pays a fee for every unit of weight, so it prefers the simplest explanation that works.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

L2 (Ridge) adds λ·Σwi^2, shrinking weights smoothly toward zero. L1 (Lasso) adds λ·Σ|wi|, driving many weights exactly to zero, producing sparse feature-selecting models.

Worked Example

Loss = MSE + λ * penalty
Weights w = [3, 0.1, -2]
L2 penalty = 3^2 + 0.1^2 + (-2)^2 = 9+0.01+4 = 13.01
L1 penalty = |3| + |0.1| + |-2| = 5.1
Larger λ => stronger shrinkage toward zero.
📝 KEY IDEA

L1 yields sparse, interpretable models by zeroing weights; L2 keeps all features but small. Elastic Net combines both. The strength λ trades bias against variance.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Too much regularization (λ too high) underfits: the model becomes too simple and biased. Too little overfits. λ must be tuned, typically by validation.

"}, "AIM-MATH/ch4/s4": {"body": "

Beyond Plain SGD

Modern optimizers accelerate and stabilize training. Momentum accumulates a running average of past gradients, smoothing the path and speeding through ravines. Adaptive methods give each parameter its own effective learning rate.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Plain SGD is a hiker taking fixed steps. Momentum is a heavy ball rolling downhill that builds speed and ignores little bumps. Adam adds smart braking on steep, jittery directions.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Adam keeps two running averages: the first moment (mean of gradients, like momentum) and the second moment (mean of squared gradients). It divides the step by the square root of the second moment, so large, noisy gradients take smaller steps.

Worked Example

Momentum: v ← β·v + (1-β)·g ,  θ ← θ - η·v
With β=0.9, past velocity persists 90% each step,
so consistent gradient directions accumulate speed
while oscillating directions cancel out.
📝 KEY IDEA

Adam = momentum (1st moment) + RMSProp-style per-parameter scaling (2nd moment) + bias correction. It is a default optimizer for much of deep learning because it needs little tuning.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Adam is not universally best: for some tasks well-tuned SGD with momentum generalizes better. Adam still needs a reasonable base learning rate; it is adaptive, not tuning-free.

"}, "AIM-MATH/intensive/s1": {"body": "

Linear Algebra Reference

💡 KEY RESULTS

Spectral theorem: a real symmetric A is orthogonally diagonalizable, A=QΛQᵀ with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors. SVD: any A=UΣVᵀ; σᵢ=√(λᵢ(AᵀA)); rank = # nonzero σ. Rank–nullity: rank+nullity=n. A is positive definite ⇔ all eigenvalues >0 ⇔ all leading principal minors >0.

⚙️ FORMULAS

det A = Πλᵢ, tr A = Σλᵢ. 2-norm condition number κ₂(A)=σ_max/σ_min. Orthogonal projector onto col(A): P=A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ, P²=P=Pᵀ, tr P = rank. Rank-1 projector onto unit u: uuᵀ. ‖A‖_F²=Σσᵢ², ‖A‖₂=σ_max. Rayleigh quotient xᵀAx/xᵀx∈[λ_min,λ_max].

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

Characteristic polynomial det(A−λI)=0 gives eigenvalues; for 2×2 use λ²−(tr)λ+det=0. Geometric multiplicity = dim null(A−λI) ≤ algebraic multiplicity. Best rank-k approx (Eckart–Young): truncate SVD; error ‖A−A_k‖₂=σ_{k+1}.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Defective matrices (geometric < algebraic multiplicity) are NOT diagonalizable, e.g. 3103. Nonsymmetric matrices may have complex eigenvalues even when real; eigenvectors need not be orthogonal. Singular values ≠ |eigenvalues| unless A is symmetric PSD.

"}, "AIM-MATH/intensive/s2": {"body": "

Matrix & Multivariable Calculus

💡 KEY RESULTS

Denominator layout: gradient is a column vector, Jacobian J has Jᵢⱼ=∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ. Hessian H=∇²f is symmetric for C² functions (Schwarz). A stationary point is a local min if H≻0, a local max if H≺0, and a saddle if H is indefinite. The gradient always points in the direction of steepest ascent, and is orthogonal to level sets.

⚙️ FORMULAS

∇(aᵀx)=a, ∇(xᵀx)=2x, ∇(xᵀAx)=(A+Aᵀ)x (=2Ax if A symmetric), Hessian =A+Aᵀ. ∇‖Ax−b‖²=2Aᵀ(Ax−b). Chain rule: ∇(g∘f)=Jfᵀ∇g. Directional derivative D_u f=∇fᵀu (u unit). d/dX tr(AX)=Aᵀ, d/dX tr(XᵀAX)=(A+Aᵀ)X, d/dX log det X = X⁻ᵀ.

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

Lagrange multipliers: at a constrained extremum ∇f=Σλᵢ∇gᵢ. Second-order Taylor: f(x+p)≈f(x)+∇fᵀp+½pᵀHp. To differentiate matrix expressions, expand to scalar sums or use the differential df=tr(Gᵀ dX) ⇒ ∂f/∂X=G.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

For nonsymmetric A, ∇(xᵀAx)=(A+Aᵀ)x, NOT 2Ax. H≻0 is sufficient but not necessary for a strict local min (e.g. x⁴ at 0). A vanishing gradient with indefinite Hessian is a saddle, not an extremum.

"}, "AIM-MATH/intensive/s3": {"body": "

Probability, Statistics & Information Theory

💡 KEY RESULTS

MLE maximizes log-likelihood; MAP adds a log-prior (Gaussian prior ⇒ ridge/L2 penalty, Laplace prior ⇒ L1). An estimator's MSE = bias² + variance. KL(p‖q)≥0 with equality iff p=q (Gibbs); it is asymmetric. Cross-entropy H(p,q)=H(p)+KL(p‖q), so cross-entropy loss upper-bounds the true entropy. Mutual information I(X;Y)=KL(p(x,y)‖p(x)p(y))≥0 measures statistical dependence and vanishes iff X⊥Y.

⚙️ FORMULAS

Gaussian KL: KL(N(μ₀,σ₀²)‖N(μ₁,σ₁²))=log(σ₁/σ₀)+(σ₀²+(μ₀−μ₁)²)/(2σ₁²)−½. Chebyshev: P(|X−μ|≥kσ)≤1/k². Markov: P(X≥a)≤E[X]/a. Var(X)=E[X²]−(E[X])². Uniform(0,1): E=½, Var=1/12. Fisher info Bernoulli =1/(p(1−p)).

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

MLE: set d/dθ Σ log p(xᵢ;θ)=0. Gaussian variance MLE is σ̂²=(1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)², biased low; the 1/(n−1) version is unbiased. Use Jensen E[g(X)]≥g(E[X]) for convex g to prove KL≥0.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

KL is not a metric (asymmetric, no triangle inequality). Uncorrelated ≠ independent (e.g. X and X² for symmetric X have covariance 0 but are dependent). The MLE variance is biased; dividing by n−1 (Bessel) restores unbiasedness.

"}, "AIM-MATH/intensive/s4": {"body": "

Convex Optimization — Theory & Convergence

💡 KEY RESULTS

f convex ⇔ (C²) ∇²f⪰0 everywhere ⇔ f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y−x). Strong convexity (m): ∇²f⪰mI. L-smoothness: ∇f is L-Lipschitz ⇔ ∇²f⪯LI. Condition number κ=L/m governs GD speed. For convex problems with Slater's condition, strong duality holds (zero duality gap).

⚙️ FORMULAS

GD step η on m-strongly-convex, L-smooth f: with η=1/L the error contracts by factor (1−m/L) per step (linear). Optimal η=2/(L+m) gives factor (κ−1)/(κ+1). Plain convex L-smooth: f(x_k)−f*≤L‖x₀−x*‖²/(2k) (O(1/k)). Divergence if η>2/L. Prox of λ‖·‖₁ = soft-threshold sign(x)max(|x|−λ,0).

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

KKT (convex, differentiable): stationarity ∇f+Σλᵢ∇gᵢ+Σνⱼ∇hⱼ=0, primal/dual feasibility, complementary slackness λᵢgᵢ=0, λᵢ≥0. For quadratics f=½xᵀAx−bᵀx the minimizer is x*=A⁻¹b, minimum −½bᵀA⁻¹b.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Convexity requires ∇²f⪰0 (PSD), not strict. x³ is not convex on R. A large κ makes GD slow — Nesterov acceleration improves iteration count from O(κ) to O(√κ). The L1 ball's corners lie on axes, promoting sparsity; the rotationally symmetric L2 ball does not.

"}, "AIM-MATH/intensive2/s1": {"body": "

SVD, Pseudoinverse & Matrix Calculus

Every real A (m×n) factors as A = UΣVᵀ with orthogonal U,V and non-negative diagonal Σ. Singular values σᵢ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse is A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ, giving the minimum-norm least-squares solution x = A⁺b.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Spectral 2-norm: ‖A‖₂ = σ_max; Frobenius: ‖A‖_F = √(Σσᵢ²) = √tr(AᵀA).
  • Spectral radius ρ(A) ≤ ‖A‖ for any induced norm, with equality only for normal matrices.
  • Rayleigh quotient R(x)=xᵀMx/xᵀx ranges over [λ_min, λ_max] for symmetric M.
  • Kronecker: eig(A⊗B) = {λᵢμⱼ}, and (A⊗B)(C⊗D)=AC⊗BD.
⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Sherman–Morrison: (A+uvᵀ)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ − (A⁻¹uvᵀA⁻¹)/(1+vᵀA⁻¹u).
  • Woodbury: (A+UCV)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ − A⁻¹U(C⁻¹+VA⁻¹U)⁻¹VA⁻¹.
  • ∇_X log det X = X⁻ᵀ; ∇_X tr(AXB) = AᵀBᵀ; ∇_X tr(XᵀAX)=(A+Aᵀ)X.
📝 TECHNIQUE

Backprop is matrix calculus: for y=Wx, if δ=∂L/∂y then ∂L/∂W = δxᵀ and ∂L/∂x = Wᵀδ. Chain rule composes Jacobians right-to-left; reverse-mode accumulates vᵀJ products cheaply.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

A matrix is positive definite iff all leading principal minors are positive (Sylvester) — checking only the diagonal or the determinant is insufficient. Also ρ(A) can be far below ‖A‖₂ for non-normal A, so small spectral radius does not bound transient growth.

"}, "AIM-MATH/intensive2/s2": {"body": "

Exponential Families, Information & Convex Optimization

An exponential family has density p(x|η)=h(x)exp(ηᵀT(x)−A(η)), where T(x) is the sufficient statistic and A(η) the log-partition. Cumulants come from A: ∇A(η)=E[T(x)], ∇²A(η)=Cov[T(x)], which is also the Fisher information in the natural parameterization.

💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Fisher information: I(θ)=E[(∂_θ log p)²]=−E[∂²_θ log p]; Cramér–Rao: Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ).
  • Jensen: for convex φ, φ(E[X]) ≤ E[φ(X)]; hence E[log X] ≤ log E[X].
  • Hoeffding: for X∈[a,b], P(|X̄−μ|≥t) ≤ 2exp(−2nt²/(b−a)²).
  • Natural gradient: ∇̃L = F⁻¹∇L — steepest descent in KL geometry, parameterization-invariant.
⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Bernoulli(p): I(p)=1/(p(1−p)); Poisson(λ): I(λ)=1/λ.
  • KL(N(μ₁,σ²)‖N(μ₂,σ²)) = (μ₁−μ₂)²/(2σ²).
  • Lagrangian L(x,λ)=f(x)+λᵀg(x); dual d(λ)=inf_x L; weak duality d*≤p*.
📝 TECHNIQUE

EM maximizes the ELBO L(q,θ)=E_q[log p(x,z)]+H(q). The E-step sets q=posterior p(z|x,θ), making the bound tight (KL=0); the M-step maximizes over θ. Each step never decreases the true log-likelihood.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Strong duality (d*=p*) needs a constraint qualification — Slater's condition (a strictly feasible point) for convex problems — it is not automatic. For SGD, the O(1/√T) rate holds for convex non-smooth objectives; strong convexity plus decaying steps buys O(1/T).

📊 FIGURE — a concentration bound you can compute
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Computing the bound

Substituting n = 100 and t = 0.1 into P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−2nt²):

2·exp(−2 × 100 × 0.1²) = 2·exp(−2 × 100 × 0.01) = 2·exp(−2)

= 2 × 0.13534 = 0.2707 ≈ 0.271

Read it correctly: this is an upper bound on the probability of being off by 0.1 or more, not the probability itself. Hoeffding makes no distributional assumption beyond boundedness, which is what makes it both widely applicable and loose.

Note the exponent's shape: t appears squared and n linearly, so halving the tolerance you want costs four times the samples.

🎯 EXAM TIP
For n = 100 in [0,1] and t = 0.1, Hoeffding gives 2e⁻² ≈ 0.271. Two things to keep straight: it is an upper bound rather than an exact probability, and because the exponent is −2nt², tightening the tolerance by half requires four times as many samples.
"}, "AIM-MATH/solving/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Matrix-vector product: for A = abcd and x = [x₁,x₂], Ax = [a·x₁+b·x₂, c·x₁+d·x₂].

Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0. For a triangular matrix the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. For symmetric abba they are a+b and a−b.

Dot product: u·v = Σ uᵢvᵢ. Cosine similarity: cos = (u·v) / (‖u‖·‖v‖), where ‖u‖ = √(Σ uᵢ²).

Gradient of f(x,y) is ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y). For f = x²+y², ∇f = (2x, 2y).

Gradient descent: x_new = x − η·∇f(x). Sigmoid σ(z)=1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) has σ'(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z)); ReLU'(z) = 1 if z>0 else 0.

Mini-example

f(x)=x², f'(x)=2x. At x=3 with η=0.1: x_new = 3 − 0.1·(2·3) = 3 − 0.6 = 2.4.

"}, "AIM-MATH/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Expectation: E[X] = Σ xᵢ·pᵢ. Variance: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².

Softmax of z: softmax(zᵢ) = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}.

Entropy (in bits, log base 2): H = −Σ pᵢ·log₂(pᵢ). Cross-entropy (bits): H(p,q) = −Σ pᵢ·log₂(qᵢ). All logs here use base 2.

Bayes' rule: P(D|+) = P(+|D)·P(D) / [ P(+|D)·P(D) + P(+|¬D)·P(¬D) ].

Losses: MSE = (1/n)·Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²; MAE = (1/n)·Σ |yᵢ − ŷᵢ|.

Mini-example

Distribution p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.25]. H = −(0.5·log₂0.5 + 0.25·log₂0.25 + 0.25·log₂0.25) = −(0.5·(−1) + 0.25·(−2) + 0.25·(−2)) = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5 bits.

"}, "AIM-MATH/solving2/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

These problems use the core linear-algebra and calculus tools behind machine learning.

Matrix-vector product

For a 2×2 matrix and vector, each output entry is a row dotted with the vector: (Ax)ᵢ = Σⱼ Aᵢⱼ xⱼ. Example: 1234·[2,1] = [1·2+2·1, 3·2+4·1] = [4, 10].

Eigenvalues of a 2×2

Solve det(A − λI) = 0. For a triangular matrix the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries. For a symmetric abba they are a+b and a−b.

Dot product & cosine similarity

a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ. Cosine similarity = (a·b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖), where ‖a‖ = √(Σ aᵢ²).

Gradients

∇f lists the partial derivatives. For f(x,y)=x²+y², ∇f=(2x, 2y). Evaluate at the given point.

Gradient-descent update

x_new = x − η∇f, subtracting the step size η times the gradient element-wise.

Activation derivatives

Sigmoid: σ' = σ(1−σ). Tanh: tanh' = 1 − tanh². ReLU: 1 for positive input, 0 otherwise. Each is written in terms of the activation's own value, so if you know the output you can get the slope directly.

"}, "AIM-MATH/solving2/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

These problems cover the probability and loss functions used to train and evaluate models. All information quantities here use logarithm base 2, so the units are bits.

Expectation & variance

E[X] = Σ xᵢ pᵢ. Variance = E[X²] − (E[X])². For a Bernoulli variable with success probability p, Var = p(1−p).

Softmax

softmax(z)ᵢ = e^(zᵢ) / Σⱼ e^(zⱼ). Exponentiate each score, then divide by the total.

Entropy (base 2)

H = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ, measured in bits. A uniform distribution over n outcomes has entropy log₂ n.

Cross-entropy (base 2)

CE = −Σ pᵢ log₂ qᵢ, where p is the true distribution and q the predicted one. For a one-hot true label, CE = −log₂(q of the true class).

Bayes posterior

P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / [P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|¬D)P(¬D)]. Combine the likelihood and prior, then normalize.

Regression error

MSE = mean of squared errors, MAE = mean of absolute errors, both averaged over the vector entries. Useful reference: log₂ 0.25 = −2 and log₂ 0.5 = −1.

"}, "AIM-MATH/aistote/s1": {"body": "

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

All three products must be added.", "2": "12 comes from adding the absolute values 2 + 4 + 6 and ignoring the negative sign on (-1)*4.", "3": "10 is the sum of the components of one vector treated as if it were the answer; a dot product multiplies pairs first."}}, {"topic": "Shapes", "text": "If A is 3x4 and B is 4x2, what is the shape of AB?", "options": ["3x4", "4x4", "3x2", "2x3"], "correct": 2, "explain": "AB is defined because the inner dimensions match (4 and 4). The product keeps the outer dimensions: 3 rows from A and 2 columns from B, so AB is 3x2.", "id": "q2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "3x4 is A's own shape; multiplying by B changes the column count to B's 2 columns.", "1": "4x4 uses the inner dimensions, which are the ones that cancel, not the ones that survive.", "3": "2x3 is the shape of (AB)^T; the rows of the product come from A, giving 3 rows first."}}, {"topic": "Validity", "text": "For A (2x3) and B (2x3), which product is undefined?", "options": ["A times B-transpose", "A times A-transpose", "B-transpose times A", "AB"], "correct": 3, "explain": "AB requires the number of columns of A (3) to equal the number of rows of B (2). They differ, so AB is undefined. Every other listed product has matching inner dimensions.", "id": "q3", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A B^T is (2x3)(3x2): inner dimensions 3 and 3 match, giving a 2x2 result.", "1": "A A^T is (2x3)(3x2): defined and yields a 2x2 matrix.", "2": "B^T A is (3x2)(2x3): inner dimensions 2 and 2 match, giving 3x3."}}, {"topic": "Commutativity", "text": "Which statement about matrix multiplication is generally TRUE?", "options": ["AB is not commutative", "AB equals A plus B", "AB always equals BA", "AB requires square matrices"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Matrix multiplication is generally non-commutative: AB and BA can differ, and one may not even be defined when the other is. Only special cases (e.g. powers of the same matrix, or the identity) commute.", "id": "q4", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "AB is a product, not a sum; A + B is a different operation that needs identical shapes.", "2": "AB = BA fails in general; for example with non-square A and B one of the two products is undefined.", "3": "Any conformable shapes work, such as a 3x4 times a 4x2; square matrices are not required."}}, {"topic": "Interpretation", "text": "A dot product of zero between two unit vectors means they are:", "options": ["Identical", "Orthogonal", "Parallel", "Opposite"], "correct": 1, "explain": "For unit vectors, u·v = cos(theta). A dot product of zero means cos(theta) = 0, so the angle is 90 degrees: the vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular).", "id": "q5", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Identical unit vectors have dot product 1, not 0.", "2": "Parallel unit vectors have dot product 1 (or -1 if opposite).", "3": "Opposite unit vectors give a dot product of -1, the minimum possible value."}}, {"topic": "NN layer", "text": "A dense layer computes y = Wx + b. If x has 5 features and y has 3 outputs, W has shape:", "options": ["5x5", "5x3", "3x5", "3x3"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Wx must be a 3-vector when x is a 5-vector, so W needs 3 rows and 5 columns: (3x5)(5x1) = 3x1. Rows count outputs, columns count inputs.", "id": "q6", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "5x5 would map 5 inputs to 5 outputs, but the layer has only 3 outputs.", "1": "5x3 has the dimensions reversed; (5x3)(5x1) is not even a defined product.", "3": "3x3 cannot accept a 5-dimensional input; the column count must equal the input size."}}, {"topic": "Identity", "text": "Multiplying any matrix A by the identity matrix I gives:", "options": ["A-transpose", "The zero matrix", "A-inverse", "A"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The identity matrix has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so every row-column dot product simply copies an entry of A. Hence AI = IA = A: the identity is the multiplicative 'one' for matrices.", "id": "q7", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Transposing is a separate operation; multiplying by I does not swap rows and columns.", "1": "Multiplying by the zero matrix gives the zero matrix; the identity leaves A unchanged.", "2": "A^-1 comes from solving AX = I, not from multiplying A by I."}}, {"topic": "Transpose", "text": "The transpose of a 3x2 matrix has shape:", "options": ["2x3", "2x2", "3x2", "3x3"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Transposing swaps the roles of rows and columns: the 3 rows become 3 columns and the 2 columns become 2 rows, giving a 2x3 matrix.", "id": "q8", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "2x2 would require dropping a row; transposing changes no entries, only their arrangement.", "2": "3x2 is the original shape; the transpose flips it.", "3": "3x3 would add entries that do not exist; a transpose has exactly the same six entries."}}, {"id": "fs2_s1_1", "topic": "Matrix multiplication", "text": "For A = [2 0; 1 3] and B = [1 4; 2 5], the product AB equals:", "options": ["[2 7; 8 19]", "[1 4; 4 20]", "[2 0; 2 15]", "[2 8; 7 19]"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Each entry is a row of A dotted with a column of B: AB[0][0] = 2*1+0*2 = 2, AB[0][1] = 2*4+0*5 = 8, AB[1][0] = 1*1+3*2 = 7, AB[1][1] = 1*4+3*5 = 19. Verified with numpy: [[2,8],[7,19]].", "distractors": {"0": "[2 7; 8 19] is the transpose of the correct product; the entries 7 and 8 are swapped.", "1": "[1 4; 4 20] mixes up which factor supplies rows: it uses columns of A instead of rows.", "2": "[2 0; 2 15] is the elementwise (Hadamard) product 2*1, 0*4, 1*2, 3*5, not matrix multiplication."}}, {"id": "fs2_s1_2", "topic": "Layer computation y = Wx + b", "text": "A layer computes y = Wx + b with W = [1 2 3; 4 5 6], x = [1, 0, -1] and b = [1, 1]. What is y?", "options": ["[4, 10]", "[-1, -1]", "[-1, -2]", "[-2, -2]"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Wx = [1*1 + 2*0 + 3*(-1), 4*1 + 5*0 + 6*(-1)] = [-2, -2]. Adding the bias b = [1, 1] gives y = [-1, -1]. Verified with numpy.", "distractors": {"0": "[4, 10] treats x as [1, 0, 1] (dropping the minus sign) and ignores the bias.", "2": "[-1, -2] adds the bias to only the first component; b is added to every output.", "3": "[-2, -2] is Wx before the bias is added; the layer computes Wx + b."}}, {"id": "fs2_s1_3", "topic": "Cost of matrix multiplication", "text": "How many scalar multiplications does the standard algorithm use to multiply a 10x20 matrix by a 20x5 matrix?", "options": ["1000", "2000", "200", "100"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The product is 10x5 = 50 entries and each entry is a length-20 dot product needing 20 multiplications: 50 * 20 = 1000. In general an (m x n)(n x p) product costs m*n*p multiplications.", "distractors": {"1": "2000 double-counts, as if each product term needed two multiplications.", "2": "200 is 10*20, the number of entries in the first matrix, not the multiplication count.", "3": "100 is 20*5, the entry count of the second matrix, not the cost of the product."}}, {"id": "fs2_s1_4", "topic": "Transpose of a product", "text": "For conformable matrices A and B, (AB)^T is equal to:", "options": ["A^T B^T", "AB", "(BA)^T", "B^T A^T"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Transposing a product reverses the order: (AB)^T = B^T A^T. Check shapes: if A is m x n and B is n x p, then B^T A^T is (p x n)(n x m) = p x m, which is exactly the shape of (AB)^T.", "distractors": {"0": "A^T B^T keeps the original order; for non-square factors it is usually not even a defined product.", "1": "AB is not its own transpose in general; transposing changes the shape from m x p to p x m.", "2": "(BA)^T equals A^T B^T, which is the wrong order, and BA itself may be undefined."}}, {"id": "fs2_s1_5", "topic": "Chained matrix shapes", "text": "A is 5x3, B is 3x7, and C is 7x2. What is the shape of ABC?", "options": ["5x2", "3x2", "5x7", "The product is undefined"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Inner dimensions cancel in sequence: (5x3)(3x7) = 5x7, then (5x7)(7x2) = 5x2. Only the first factor's rows and the last factor's columns survive.", "distractors": {"1": "3x2 uses A's column count instead of its row count; rows of the product come from A's 5 rows.", "2": "5x7 is the shape of AB alone; multiplying by C changes the columns to 2.", "3": "The product is defined because every adjacent pair has matching inner dimensions (3 with 3, 7 with 7)."}}], "AIM-MATH/ch1/s2": [{"topic": "Span", "text": "The span of a single nonzero vector in 3D is a:", "options": ["Sphere", "Line through the origin", "Plane", "Point"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The span of one nonzero vector v is the set of all multiples c*v. Those points form a line through the origin (c = 0 gives the origin itself).", "id": "q1", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A sphere is not closed under scaling, so it cannot be a span.", "2": "A plane needs two independent vectors; one vector only gives one direction.", "3": "A single point (the origin) is the span of the zero vector only; a nonzero v can be scaled to reach infinitely many points."}}, {"topic": "Independence", "text": "Vectors are linearly independent when c1v1+...+cnvn=0 has:", "options": ["No solution", "Infinitely many solutions", "Only the all-zero solution", "Exactly two solutions"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Linear independence means no vector can be written from the others, which is equivalent to saying the only way to combine them into the zero vector is with all coefficients zero.", "id": "q2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "c1 = ... = cn = 0 is always a solution, so 'no solution' never happens.", "1": "Infinitely many solutions is exactly the dependent case: a nontrivial combination gives zero.", "3": "Solution sets of linear homogeneous systems are subspaces; they contain either one solution or infinitely many, never exactly two."}}, {"topic": "Basis", "text": "A basis for a vector space must be:", "options": ["All unit vectors", "Orthogonal only", "As large as possible", "Independent and spanning"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A basis must span the space (reach every vector) and be linearly independent (no redundancy). It is the smallest spanning set and the largest independent set.", "id": "q3", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Basis vectors can have any nonzero length; unit length is a convenience, not a requirement.", "1": "Orthogonality is optional; {[1,0],[1,1]} is a perfectly good basis of R^2.", "2": "A basis is as small as possible while still spanning; adding vectors would create dependence."}}, {"topic": "Dimension", "text": "How many vectors are in any basis of R^4?", "options": ["4", "5", "16", "3"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The dimension of R^4 is 4, and every basis of a finite-dimensional space has exactly dim-many vectors. Fewer cannot span; more cannot be independent.", "id": "q4", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Five vectors in R^4 are always linearly dependent, so they cannot form a basis.", "2": "16 = 4*4 is the number of entries in a 4x4 matrix, not the dimension of R^4.", "3": "Three vectors span at most a 3-dimensional subspace and cannot reach all of R^4."}}, {"topic": "Rank", "text": "The rank of a matrix equals the number of:", "options": ["Rows", "Linearly independent columns", "Zero entries", "Columns"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Rank is the dimension of the column space, i.e. the number of linearly independent columns. The row rank is the same number, so it is also the number of independent rows.", "id": "q5", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The number of rows is only an upper bound on rank; a 5x3 matrix has rank at most 3.", "2": "Zero entries have nothing to do with rank; a matrix full of nonzeros can still have rank 1.", "3": "The number of columns is an upper bound; columns that are multiples of others do not add rank."}}, {"topic": "Redundancy", "text": "Three vectors in R^2 are always:", "options": ["Orthogonal", "A basis", "Linearly dependent", "Independent"], "correct": 2, "explain": "R^2 has dimension 2, so any set of more than 2 vectors in it must be linearly dependent: at least one is a combination of the others.", "id": "q6", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Three vectors in the plane cannot all be mutually orthogonal; at most two can be.", "1": "A basis of R^2 has exactly 2 vectors; three is too many.", "3": "Independence of three vectors would require at least a 3-dimensional space."}}, {"topic": "Subspace", "text": "Which set is NOT a subspace of R^2?", "options": ["A line through the origin", "The origin alone", "All of R^2", "A line not through the origin"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A subspace must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scaling. A line that misses the origin fails immediately, since 0 times any point on it gives the origin, which is not on the line.", "id": "q7", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A line through the origin is closed under scaling and addition, so it is a subspace.", "1": "The zero subspace {0} is a valid (trivial) subspace.", "2": "R^2 is a subspace of itself."}}, {"topic": "ML link", "text": "In ML, low matrix rank often signals that features are:", "options": ["Redundant or correlated", "Independent", "Normally distributed", "Perfectly scaled"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Low rank means some columns (features) are linear combinations of others, so the columns carry redundant, correlated information. This is the situation PCA and regularization address.", "id": "q8", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Independent features would make the columns independent and the rank full, not low.", "2": "Rank says nothing about the distribution of values, only about linear relationships between columns.", "3": "Scaling a feature does not change rank; a perfectly scaled matrix can still be low rank."}}, {"id": "fs2_s2_1", "topic": "Rank computation", "text": "What is the rank of the matrix [1 2; 2 4]?", "options": ["4", "0", "1", "2"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Row 2 = 2 * row 1, so the rows span a single line; equivalently column 2 = 2 * column 1. One independent direction means rank 1 (numpy.linalg.matrix_rank confirms 1).", "distractors": {"0": "4 is the number of entries, not the rank; rank never exceeds the smaller dimension, here 2.", "1": "Rank 0 is only for the zero matrix; this matrix has nonzero entries.", "3": "Rank 2 would need independent rows, but the second row is exactly twice the first (determinant 1*4 - 2*2 = 0)."}}, {"id": "fs2_s2_2", "topic": "Membership in a span", "text": "Which vector lies in span{[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]}?", "options": ["[2, 3, 5]", "[2, 3, 4]", "[1, 2, 1]", "[1, 1, 1]"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Any combination a*[1,0,1] + b*[0,1,1] = [a, b, a+b], so a vector is in the span iff its third coordinate equals the sum of the first two. [2,3,5] works: 5 = 2 + 3, with a = 2, b = 3.", "distractors": {"1": "[2,3,4] fails the test: 2 + 3 = 5, not 4.", "2": "[1,2,1] fails: 1 + 2 = 3, not 1.", "3": "[1,1,1] fails: 1 + 1 = 2, not 1."}}, {"id": "fs2_s2_3", "topic": "Maximum possible rank", "text": "What is the largest possible rank of a 5x3 matrix?", "options": ["3", "8", "15", "5"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Rank is at most the number of rows and at most the number of columns, so rank <= min(5, 3) = 3. A 5x3 matrix with three independent columns achieves rank 3.", "distractors": {"1": "8 = 5 + 3 has no meaning here; rank cannot exceed either dimension.", "2": "15 = 5*3 is the number of entries, not a bound on rank.", "3": "Rank 5 is impossible with only 3 columns; at most 3 of anything can be independent."}}, {"id": "fs2_s2_4", "topic": "Rank-nullity theorem", "text": "A matrix A is 4x6 and has rank 4. What is the dimension of its null space?", "options": ["6", "0", "2", "4"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Rank-nullity: rank + nullity = number of columns. Here 4 + nullity = 6, so the null space has dimension 2.", "distractors": {"0": "6 is the total number of columns, not what is left after removing the rank.", "1": "Nullity 0 would require full column rank 6, impossible for a matrix with only 4 rows.", "3": "4 is the rank (and the number of rows), not the nullity; subtract it from 6."}}, {"id": "fs2_s2_5", "topic": "Dimension of a span", "text": "What is the dimension of span{[1,0,0], [0,1,0], [1,1,0], [2,2,0]}?", "options": ["2", "1", "4", "3"], "correct": 0, "explain": "[1,1,0] = [1,0,0] + [0,1,0] and [2,2,0] = 2*[1,1,0], so only the first two vectors are independent. Every vector has third coordinate 0, so the span is the xy-plane, dimension 2 (matrix_rank = 2).", "distractors": {"1": "Dimension 1 would mean all four vectors are multiples of one another, but [1,0,0] and [0,1,0] are not.", "2": "Four vectors do not automatically give dimension 4; the last two are combinations of the first two.", "3": "Dimension 3 is impossible because every vector has a zero third coordinate, so the span lies in a plane."}}], "AIM-MATH/ch1/s3": [{"topic": "Definition", "text": "If Av = λv with v nonzero, then v is a(n):", "options": ["Null vector", "Eigenvector with eigenvalue λ", "Basis vector", "Orthogonal complement"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Av = lambda*v with v nonzero says A only stretches v (by the factor lambda) without changing its direction. That is exactly the definition of an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda.", "id": "q1_d3", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A null vector would satisfy Av = 0, i.e. lambda = 0, and the question says v is nonzero and lambda is arbitrary.", "2": "Basis vectors need not be stretched by A; eigenvectors are special directions, not any basis.", "3": "The orthogonal complement is a subspace perpendicular to something, unrelated to this equation."}}, {"topic": "Char equation", "text": "Eigenvalues are found by solving:", "options": ["A-transpose = A", "trace(A) = 0", "det(A - λI) = 0", "Av = 0"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Av = lambda*v can be rewritten (A - lambda*I)v = 0. A nonzero solution v exists only if A - lambda*I is singular, i.e. det(A - lambda*I) = 0, the characteristic equation.", "id": "q2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A^T = A says the matrix is symmetric; it is a property, not an equation to solve for lambda.", "1": "trace(A) = 0 is a single number condition; the trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues, not the eigenvalues themselves.", "3": "Av = 0 finds the null space (eigenvalue 0 only); the general case needs lambda in the equation."}}, {"topic": "Diagonal", "text": "The eigenvalues of diag(4, 7) are:", "options": ["28 and 1", "4 and 4", "11 and 0", "4 and 7"], "correct": 3, "explain": "For a diagonal matrix, A e_i = (diagonal entry) * e_i, so each standard basis vector is an eigenvector and the diagonal entries 4 and 7 are the eigenvalues.", "id": "q3", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "28 and 1 come from taking the product 4*7 and a leftover; the determinant is 28, but that is the product of eigenvalues, not an eigenvalue.", "1": "4 and 4 repeats one entry; each diagonal entry is its own eigenvalue.", "2": "11 and 0: 11 is the trace (sum of eigenvalues), not an eigenvalue."}}, {"topic": "Trace", "text": "For a 2x2 matrix, the sum of eigenvalues equals the:", "options": ["Trace", "Largest entry", "Determinant", "Rank"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The characteristic polynomial of a 2x2 matrix is lambda^2 - (trace)lambda + det, so the two roots add to the trace and multiply to the determinant.", "id": "q4", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "The largest entry has no general relation to the eigenvalues.", "2": "The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues, not their sum.", "3": "Rank counts nonzero eigenvalues for diagonalizable matrices; it is not their sum."}}, {"topic": "Determinant", "text": "The product of all eigenvalues equals the matrix's:", "options": ["Norm", "Determinant", "Trace", "Rank"], "correct": 1, "explain": "det(A) equals the product of the eigenvalues (with multiplicity). For a 2x2 this is visible in lambda^2 - (trace)lambda + det = 0, where the constant term is the product of the roots.", "id": "q5", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Norms measure size; the spectral norm is the largest singular value, not a product of eigenvalues.", "2": "The trace is the sum of eigenvalues, not the product.", "3": "Rank counts nonzero eigenvalues; it is not their product."}}, {"topic": "PCA link", "text": "In PCA, the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points along the direction of:", "options": ["The mean", "Zero correlation", "Maximum variance", "Least variance"], "correct": 2, "explain": "PCA diagonalizes the covariance matrix. The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is the direction along which projected data has the largest variance, and that eigenvalue is the variance along it.", "id": "q6", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The mean is subtracted before PCA; it is a point, not a direction of spread.", "1": "Zero correlation is a property between components after rotation, not the direction of the top eigenvector.", "3": "Least variance corresponds to the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue."}}, {"topic": "Zero eigenvalue", "text": "A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is:", "options": ["Invertible", "Orthogonal", "Symmetric", "Singular (non-invertible)"], "correct": 3, "explain": "det(A) is the product of the eigenvalues, so a zero eigenvalue forces det(A) = 0. A matrix with zero determinant has no inverse: some nonzero v satisfies Av = 0.", "id": "q7", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Invertible matrices have all eigenvalues nonzero, since their determinant is nonzero.", "1": "Orthogonal matrices have eigenvalues of absolute value 1, never 0.", "2": "Symmetric matrices can be invertible or not; symmetry is unrelated to having a zero eigenvalue."}}, {"topic": "Scaling", "text": "If v is an eigenvector of A, then 5v is:", "options": ["An eigenvector with the same eigenvalue", "An eigenvector with 5x the eigenvalue", "The zero vector", "Not an eigenvector"], "correct": 0, "explain": "If Av = lambda*v then A(5v) = 5(Av) = 5*lambda*v = lambda*(5v). Scaling the vector does not change the stretch factor, so 5v is an eigenvector for the same eigenvalue.", "id": "q8", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "The eigenvalue is a property of the direction; scaling v by 5 scales both sides of Av = lambda v equally, leaving lambda unchanged.", "2": "5v is nonzero whenever v is nonzero.", "3": "Every nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector; the eigenspace is closed under scaling."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_1", "topic": "Eigenvalues of a symmetric 2x2", "text": "Solving the characteristic equation det(A - λI) = 0 for A = [5 2; 2 5] yields which pair of values?", "options": ["5 and 2", "7 and 3", "5 and 5", "7 and -3"], "correct": 1, "explain": "det(A - lambda I) = (5 - lambda)^2 - 2*2 = 0, so (5 - lambda)^2 = 4 and 5 - lambda = +/-2, giving lambda = 3 and lambda = 7. Check: trace 10 = 7 + 3 and det 21 = 7*3. numpy.linalg.eigvals confirms [7, 3].", "distractors": {"0": "5 and 2 are just the matrix entries; the off-diagonal 2 shifts the eigenvalues away from 5.", "2": "5 and 5 would be right only if the off-diagonal entries were zero.", "3": "7 and -3 has the wrong sign on the second value: the determinant 25 - 4 = 21 must equal the product, and 7*(-3) = -21."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_2", "topic": "Eigenvalues of a triangular matrix", "text": "The eigenvalues of A = [2 5; 0 -3] are:", "options": ["2 and 5", "2 and -3", "-1 and 6", "5 and -3"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A is upper triangular, so det(A - lambda I) = (2 - lambda)(-3 - lambda): the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 2 and -3. Check: trace -1 = 2 + (-3), det -6 = 2*(-3).", "distractors": {"0": "2 and 5 uses the top row; the off-diagonal 5 never appears in the characteristic polynomial of a triangular matrix.", "2": "-1 and 6: -1 is the trace and -6 is the determinant, not the eigenvalues themselves.", "3": "5 and -3 uses the second column instead of the diagonal."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_3", "topic": "Eigenvalues of a matrix power", "text": "If A has eigenvalues 2 and 5, the eigenvalues of A^2 are:", "options": ["4 and 10", "10 and 25", "2 and 5", "4 and 25"], "correct": 3, "explain": "If Av = lambda v, then A^2 v = A(lambda v) = lambda(Av) = lambda^2 v. The eigenvectors stay the same and the eigenvalues square: 2^2 = 4 and 5^2 = 25.", "distractors": {"0": "4 and 10 doubles the second eigenvalue instead of squaring it; A^2 is not 2A.", "1": "10 and 25 multiplies the eigenvalues together for the first entry; each eigenvalue is squared on its own.", "2": "2 and 5 are the eigenvalues of A, not of A^2; squaring the matrix squares them."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_4", "topic": "Eigenvalue for a given eigenvector", "text": "For A = [3 1; 1 3], the eigenvalue associated with the eigenvector [1, -1] is:", "options": ["4", "3", "2", "-2"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Multiply: A[1,-1] = [3*1 + 1*(-1), 1*1 + 3*(-1)] = [2, -2] = 2*[1, -1]. The stretch factor is 2, so the eigenvalue for this eigenvector is 2 (the other eigenvector [1,1] has eigenvalue 4).", "distractors": {"0": "4 is the eigenvalue of the other eigenvector [1, 1], where A[1,1] = [4, 4].", "1": "3 is just the diagonal entry; the off-diagonal 1 shifts the eigenvalues to 3 +/- 1.", "3": "-2 has the wrong sign: A[1,-1] = [2,-2] = +2 times [1,-1], not -2 times it."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_5", "topic": "Trace and determinant give eigenvalues", "text": "A 2x2 matrix has trace 7 and determinant 12. Its eigenvalues are:", "options": ["7 and 12", "1 and 12", "3 and 4", "2 and 6"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Eigenvalues of a 2x2 satisfy lambda^2 - (trace)lambda + det = lambda^2 - 7 lambda + 12 = (lambda - 3)(lambda - 4) = 0. Roots 3 and 4 sum to 7 and multiply to 12 (sympy solve confirms [3, 4]).", "distractors": {"0": "7 and 12 are the trace and determinant themselves, not the roots; 7 + 12 = 19, not 7.", "1": "1 and 12 multiply to 12 but sum to 13, not 7.", "3": "2 and 6 multiply to 12 but sum to 8, not 7; both conditions must hold."}}], "AIM-MATH/ch1/s4": [{"topic": "Orthogonal", "text": "Two vectors are orthogonal exactly when their dot product is:", "options": ["One", "Zero", "Negative", "Their length product"], "correct": 1, "explain": "By definition two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero. Starting in state 1 for sure, the chain stays with probability 0.8 and moves with probability 0.2 (numpy confirms).", "id": "q6_d2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "[0.5, 0.5] is not a row of P and does not arise from a single step here.", "1": "[0.4, 0.6] is row 2, the result of starting in state 2 ([0, 1] P).", "3": "[1, 0] is the starting distribution; after a step probability leaks to state 2."}}, {"topic": "Application", "text": "Which algorithm is built on a Markov chain over web pages?", "options": ["K-means", "Backprop", "Naive Bayes", "PageRank"], "correct": 3, "explain": "PageRank imagines a random surfer clicking links: the pages are states, the links define transition probabilities, and a page's rank is its stationary probability under that Markov chain.", "id": "q7", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "K-means is a clustering algorithm with no transition structure.", "1": "Backprop computes gradients for neural networks.", "2": "Naive Bayes is a classifier built on conditional independence, not on state transitions."}}, {"topic": "Memoryless", "text": "A key feature captured by Markov chains is being:", "options": ["Memoryless", "Deterministic only", "Continuous only", "History-dependent"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Markov chains are memoryless: the next state depends only on the current one, so the entire past can be forgotten once you know where the chain is now.", "id": "q8", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Markov chains are stochastic; transitions are random, not deterministic.", "2": "Markov chains can have discrete state spaces and discrete time; continuity is not required.", "3": "History-dependence is the opposite of the Markov property."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_1", "topic": "Two-step distribution", "text": "With P = [0.9 0.1; 0.5 0.5] and starting distribution x = [1, 0], the distribution after two steps is:", "options": ["[0.7, 0.3]", "[0.81, 0.19]", "[0.9, 0.1]", "[0.86, 0.14]"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Step 1: [1, 0] P = [0.9, 0.1]. Step 2: [0.9(0.9) + 0.1(0.5), 0.9(0.1) + 0.1(0.5)] = [0.81 + 0.05, 0.09 + 0.05] = [0.86, 0.14] (numpy: x @ P @ P).", "distractors": {"0": "[0.7, 0.3] is the stationary-ish guess, not the exact two-step result.", "1": "[0.81, 0.19] squares only the stay probability and forgets the return path from state 2 (0.1 * 0.5 = 0.05).", "2": "[0.9, 0.1] is the distribution after one step, not two."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_2", "topic": "Stationary distribution", "text": "The stationary distribution of P = [0.8 0.2; 0.4 0.6] is:", "options": ["[1/2, 1/2]", "[0.8, 0.2]", "[1/3, 2/3]", "[2/3, 1/3]"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Solve pi P = pi: 0.8 pi1 + 0.4 pi2 = pi1 gives 0.4 pi2 = 0.2 pi1, so pi1 = 2 pi2. With pi1 + pi2 = 1: pi = [2/3, 1/3]. Check: [2/3, 1/3] P = [0.8(2/3) + 0.4(1/3), 0.2(2/3) + 0.6(1/3)] = [2/3, 1/3].", "distractors": {"0": "[1/2, 1/2] P = [0.6, 0.4], which is not [1/2, 1/2], so it is not stationary.", "1": "[0.8, 0.2] is the first row of P (the one-step result from state 1), not the fixed point: [0.8, 0.2] P = [0.72, 0.28].", "2": "[1/3, 2/3] has the states reversed; state 1 is stickier (0.8 stay) so it must carry more mass."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_3", "topic": "Completing a transition row", "text": "A row of a transition matrix reads [0.3, 0.2, ?]. The missing entry must be:", "options": ["1.0", "0.5", "0.4", "0.25"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Each row of a transition matrix is a probability distribution over the next state and must sum to 1, so the missing entry is 1 - 0.3 - 0.2 = 0.5.", "distractors": {"0": "1.0 would make the row sum 1.5, impossible for probabilities.", "2": "0.4 gives a row sum of 0.9; some probability would be unaccounted for.", "3": "0.25 gives a row sum of 0.75, again leaving probability missing."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_4", "topic": "Interpreting powers of P", "text": "The (i, j) entry of P^n gives the probability that the chain:", "options": ["is in state j after exactly n steps, having started in state i", "visits state j at least once within n steps", "stays in state i for n steps", "reaches its stationary distribution in n steps"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Matrix multiplication sums over all intermediate states: (P^2)_ij = sum_k P_ik P_kj is the probability of going i -> k -> j for any k, and by induction (P^n)_ij is the probability of being in j exactly n steps after starting in i.", "distractors": {"1": "'At least once' would be a hitting probability, which requires a different calculation, not a matrix power.", "2": "Staying in i for n steps is (P_ii)^n, a single-entry power, not the (i, j) entry of P^n.", "3": "Convergence to stationarity is a limit as n grows; P^n itself gives exact n-step probabilities."}}, {"id": "fs2_s3_5", "topic": "Spectrum of a stochastic matrix", "text": "Every transition matrix has an eigenvalue equal to:", "options": ["1", "the number of states", "0", "-1"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Each row sums to 1, so P times the all-ones column vector 1 gives 1 again: P 1 = 1 * 1. Hence 1 is an eigenvalue of every stochastic matrix, and it is the largest in absolute value (numpy eigvals of [0.8 0.2; 0.4 0.6] are [1, 0.4]).", "distractors": {"1": "The number of states is not an eigenvalue in general; for the 2-state example the eigenvalues are 1 and 0.4.", "2": "0 is an eigenvalue only if P is singular, which need not happen.", "3": "-1 can occur for periodic chains but is not guaranteed; 1 is."}}], "AIM-MATH/ch3/s4": [{"topic": "Null", "text": "The null hypothesis typically represents:", "options": ["The p-value", "No effect / default assumption", "The effect we hope to find", "A confidence interval"], "correct": 1, "explain": "H0 is the default or skeptical claim, usually 'no effect' or 'no difference' (e.g. the new model is no better). The test asks whether the data are surprising enough to reject it.", "id": "q1", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The p-value is a number computed from the data under H0, not the hypothesis itself.", "2": "The effect we hope to find is the alternative hypothesis H1.", "3": "A confidence interval is an estimate of a parameter, not a hypothesis."}}, {"topic": "p-value", "text": "A p-value is the probability of data this extreme, assuming:", "options": ["The prior is uniform", "H1 is true", "H0 is true", "The sample is infinite"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H0 is true). It is computed entirely under the assumption that the null hypothesis holds.", "id": "q2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Priors belong to Bayesian analysis; classical p-values use none.", "1": "Computing under H1 would give power, not the p-value.", "3": "Sample size is finite; the p-value uses the actual sample, not an infinite one."}}, {"topic": "Threshold", "text": "If α = 0.05 and p = 0.02, you should:", "options": ["Fail to reject H0", "Increase α", "Accept H1 as certain", "Reject H0"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The decision rule is: reject H0 when p <= alpha. Since 0.02 < 0.05, the data are unlikely enough under H0 to reject it at the 5% level.", "id": "q3", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Failing to reject applies when p > alpha; here p is below alpha.", "1": "Alpha must be fixed before seeing the data; changing it afterward is p-hacking.", "2": "Rejecting H0 supports H1 but never makes it certain; there is still a 5% false-positive risk."}}, {"topic": "Misread", "text": "A p-value does NOT tell you the probability that:", "options": ["H0 is true", "You would see this by chance under H0", "The result is at least this extreme", "Data is extreme under H0"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The p-value is P(data | H0), not P(H0 | data). Turning it into the probability that the null is true would require a prior and Bayes' theorem.", "id": "q4", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "'Seeing this by chance under H0' is exactly what the p-value quantifies.", "2": "'At least this extreme' is the tail event the p-value measures.", "3": "Extremeness under H0 is the p-value's definition."}}, {"topic": "Confidence interval", "text": "A 95% confidence interval provides:", "options": ["The p-value", "A range of plausible values", "The exact truth", "A single best guess"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A 95% confidence interval is a range computed so that, over repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter. It conveys both an estimate and its uncertainty.", "id": "q5", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A p-value is a single probability for a test, not an interval.", "2": "The exact truth is unknown; the interval expresses uncertainty about it.", "3": "A single best guess is the point estimate; the interval adds a margin around it."}}, {"topic": "Non-significant", "text": "Failing to reject H0 means:", "options": ["The p-value is zero", "H0 is proven true", "Insufficient evidence against H0", "H1 is impossible"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. p > alpha means the data are compatible with H0, but a small effect could still exist and go undetected (a Type II error).", "id": "q6", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A p-value of zero would be overwhelming evidence against H0, the opposite situation.", "1": "Tests cannot prove H0; they can only fail to find evidence against it.", "3": "H1 remains possible; the test simply lacked the power to demonstrate it."}}, {"topic": "Multiple testing", "text": "Running many tests without correction tends to increase:", "options": ["The prior", "Sample size", "Statistical power", "False positives"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Each test at alpha = 0.05 has a 5% false-positive chance under H0. Running many tests multiplies the opportunities: with 10 independent null tests, P(at least one false positive) = 1 - 0.95^10 ≈ 40%.", "id": "q7", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Priors are not part of classical testing and do not change with more tests.", "1": "Sample size is fixed by the data collection, not by how many tests you run.", "2": "Power is about detecting true effects; multiple testing inflates false positives, not power."}}, {"topic": "ML eval", "text": "When comparing two models, error bars mainly show whether a gain is:", "options": ["Beyond random noise", "Larger than the dataset", "Exactly 5%", "Always significant"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Error bars (e.g. standard errors across seeds or folds) show the spread from randomness. If the two models' bars overlap heavily, the difference could be noise; a gain clearly outside the bars is more believable.", "id": "q8", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Error bars are in the units of the metric, unrelated to dataset size.", "2": "No fixed percentage is implied; the bars show the estimated variability.", "3": "Significance is a conclusion drawn from the bars, not something they guarantee."}}, {"id": "fs2_s4_1", "topic": "Applying a significance threshold", "text": "A test yields p = 0.08 with a pre-set threshold α = 0.05. The correct conclusion is:", "options": ["reject H0; the result is significant", "accept H0 as proven true", "fail to reject H0; the result is not statistically significant", "lower α to 0.10 so the result becomes significant"], "correct": 2, "explain": "p = 0.08 > alpha = 0.05, so the observed data are not rare enough under H0 to reject it: the result is not statistically significant. This is a failure to reject, not proof of H0.", "distractors": {"0": "Rejecting requires p <= alpha; 0.08 exceeds 0.05.", "1": "A non-significant result never proves H0; it only fails to contradict it.", "3": "Raising alpha after seeing p (to 0.10, which is also not 'lower') is p-hacking; the threshold is fixed in advance."}}, {"id": "fs2_s4_2", "topic": "Type I error", "text": "A Type I error occurs when you:", "options": ["compute the p-value incorrectly", "choose the wrong test statistic", "fail to reject H0 even though H0 is false", "reject H0 even though H0 is true"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A Type I error is a false positive: concluding there is an effect (rejecting H0) when in fact H0 is true. Its probability under H0 is the significance level alpha.", "distractors": {"0": "Miscomputing a p-value is a calculation mistake, not an error type in the testing framework.", "1": "Choosing a poor statistic affects power but is not the definition of a Type I error.", "2": "Failing to reject a false H0 is a Type II error (false negative)."}}, {"id": "fs2_s4_3", "topic": "Type II error", "text": "Failing to reject H0 when the alternative is actually true is called:", "options": ["a Type II error", "a Type I error", "a p-hacking error", "a confidence error"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Missing a real effect (not rejecting H0 when H1 is true) is a Type II error, or false negative. Its probability is beta, and power = 1 - beta.", "distractors": {"1": "A Type I error is the opposite mistake: rejecting a true H0.", "2": "p-hacking is a research-practice problem, not a formal error type.", "3": "'Confidence error' is not a standard term."}}, {"id": "fs2_s4_4", "topic": "Effect of sample size", "text": "Increasing the sample size, all else equal, tends to:", "options": ["widen the confidence interval and increase power", "leave both the interval width and power unchanged", "narrow the confidence interval and increase power", "narrow the confidence interval and decrease power"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Standard errors shrink like 1/sqrt(n), so confidence intervals narrow. The Bonferroni-corrected per-test threshold is:", "options": ["0.05", "0.10", "0.005", "0.5"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Bonferroni divides the family-wise alpha by the number of tests: 0.05 / 10 = 0.005 per test. Without correction, 10 null tests at 0.05 give 1 - 0.95^10 ≈ 40% chance of at least one false positive.", "distractors": {"0": "0.05 is the uncorrected per-test level, which lets the family-wise error rate balloon to about 40%.", "1": "0.10 doubles the threshold, making false positives more likely, the opposite of a correction.", "3": "0.5 multiplies by the number of tests instead of dividing."}}], "AIM-MATH/ch4/s1": [{"topic": "Update rule", "text": "In θ ← θ − η·∇L, the term η is the:", "options": ["Loss", "Learning rate", "Gradient", "Momentum"], "correct": 1, "explain": "theta <- theta - eta ∇L moves against the gradient; eta, the learning rate, sets how large each step is. Too large diverges, too small crawls.", "id": "q1", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The loss L is what is being minimized; eta scales the step taken to reduce it.", "2": "The gradient is ∇L, the direction term; eta multiplies it.", "3": "Momentum is an extra velocity term in other optimizers, not the plain step-size factor."}}, {"topic": "SGD", "text": "Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient using:", "options": ["No data", "The full dataset", "One or a few examples", "The Hessian"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Stochastic gradient descent replaces the full-dataset gradient with an estimate from one example (or a small mini-batch). The estimate is noisy but far cheaper, so many more updates fit in the same time.", "id": "q2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Without data there is no gradient to estimate.", "1": "Using the full dataset each step is batch gradient descent, not SGD.", "3": "The Hessian holds second derivatives and is not used by first-order SGD."}}, {"topic": "Mini-batch", "text": "Mini-batch gradient descent is popular because it:", "options": ["Uses no gradients", "Requires the whole dataset each step", "Ignores the learning rate", "Balances speed and stability"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A mini-batch (e.g. 32-256 examples) averages away much of single-sample noise while staying cheap enough for frequent updates and mapping well to GPU parallelism. At a saddle or plateau the true gradient is near zero, but the noise can kick the parameters off the flat region and let descent resume.", "id": "q7", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Nothing in SGD guarantees the global optimum for non-convex losses.", "1": "Noise perturbs gradients; it does not eliminate them.", "2": "A learning rate is still required to scale each noisy step."}}, {"topic": "Too small", "text": "A learning rate that is too small causes:", "options": ["Very slow convergence", "Divergence", "Exploding gradients", "Overshooting"], "correct": 0, "explain": "With a tiny eta each step covers only a small fraction of the distance to the minimum, so many iterations are needed; training is stable but painfully slow.", "id": "q8", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Divergence is caused by a learning rate that is too large.", "2": "Exploding gradients come from the network's dynamics or an oversized step, not a small one.", "3": "Overshooting requires steps that are too big; small steps undershoot."}}, {"id": "fs2_s1_1", "topic": "Two gradient descent steps", "text": "Minimizing L(θ) = θ^2 (gradient 2θ) with η = 0.3 from θ = 2, the value of θ after two steps is:", "options": ["1.40", "0.32", "0.80", "0.64"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Gradient 2 theta.
