Here that set is {1*2, 1*5, 3*2, 3*5} = {2, 5, 6, 15}, so the maximum is 15 (numpy eigvals of kron(diag(1,3), diag(2,5)) returns exactly 2, 5, 6, 15).", "id": "q9", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "8 would be a SUM (3 + 5), which is the rule for the Kronecker SUM A⊗I + I⊗B, not the Kronecker product.", "1": "10 = 2 + 3 + 5 mixes sums and products; Kronecker eigenvalues are pure pairwise products.", "2": "30 = 1*3*2*5 multiplies all four eigenvalues together, which gives the determinant-like quantity, not a single eigenvalue."}}, {"topic": "Exponential family", "text": "For an exponential family, ∇²A(η) (Hessian of the log-partition) equals:", "options": ["Cov[T(x)], the Fisher information", "the entropy", "0", "E[T(x)]"], "correct": 0, "explain": "In an exponential family p(x) = h(x) exp(eta·T(x) - A(eta)), the log-partition A is a cumulant generating function: its gradient is E[T(x)] and its Hessian is Cov[T(x)]. In natural coordinates that covariance IS the Fisher information matrix.", "id": "q2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "The entropy is a different functional of the distribution and is a scalar, whereas the Hessian is a matrix.", "2": "A zero Hessian would make A linear, which happens only in degenerate families; in general Cov[T(x)] is positive semidefinite and nonzero.", "3": "E[T(x)] is the FIRST derivative (the gradient) of A, not the second."}}, {"topic": "SVD", "text": "For A = [[3,0],[4,5]], the largest singular value σ_max equals:", "options": ["5", "7", "√30", "√45 = 3√5 ≈ 6.708"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA. AᵀA = [[9+16, 20],[20, 25]] = [[25,20],[20,25]], whose characteristic polynomial is lambda^2 - 50 lambda + 225 with roots 45 and 5 (numpy eigvalsh agrees). So sigma_max = sqrt(45) = 3 sqrt5 ≈ 6.708.", "id": "q1", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "5 is the largest eigenvalue of A itself (A is triangular, eigenvalues 3 and 5); for a non-symmetric A the singular values are not the absolute eigenvalues.", "1": "7 is close to the Frobenius norm sqrt(9+16+25) = sqrt50 ≈ 7.071, which is the root-sum of ALL squared singular values, not the largest one.", "2": "sqrt30 ≈ 5.477 is not a root of lambda^2 - 50 lambda + 225; the two roots are 45 and 5."}}, {"topic": "Fisher information", "text": "The Fisher information of a Bernoulli(p) sample at p=0.25 is:", "options": ["0.1875", "3", "4", "16/3 ≈ 5.333"], "correct": 3, "explain": "For a single Bernoulli(p) observation the Fisher information is I(p) = 1/(p(1-p)). At p = 0.25 that is 1/(0.25 * 0.75) = 1/0.1875 = 16/3 ≈ 5.333. Information is highest near p = 0 or 1 and lowest (I = 4) at p = 0.5.", "id": "q1_d2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "0.1875 = p(1-p) is the VARIANCE of a single Bernoulli draw; the Fisher information is its reciprocal.", "1": "3 does not arise here; 1/0.1875 = 5.333, and 3 would need p(1-p) = 1/3, which is impossible since p(1-p) <= 0.25.", "2": "4 = 1/0.25 is the Fisher information at p = 0.5, where p(1-p) is largest and information is at its MINIMUM."}}, {"topic": "Positive definiteness", "text": "Which condition is NECESSARY AND SUFFICIENT for a symmetric matrix to be positive definite?", "options": ["All diagonal entries positive", "Trace positive", "Determinant positive", "All leading principal minors positive"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Sylvester's criterion: a symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if every leading principal minor (the determinants of the top-left 1x1, 2x2, ..., nxn blocks) is strictly positive. This is both necessary and sufficient; the other conditions are necessary but not sufficient.", "id": "q5", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Positive diagonal entries are necessary but not sufficient: [[1,2],[2,1]] has positive diagonal yet eigenvalues 3 and -1.", "1": "A positive trace only says the eigenvalues sum to something positive; diag(3, -1) has trace 2 but is indefinite.", "2": "A positive determinant only says an even number of eigenvalues are negative; diag(-1, -1) has determinant 1 and is negative definite."}}, {"topic": "Sufficient statistic", "text": "For N(μ,σ²) with both unknown, a sufficient statistic for the sample is:", "options": ["the maximum value", "(Σxᵢ, Σxᵢ²)", "the sample mean only", "the sample median"], "correct": 1, "explain": "By the factorization theorem the likelihood of N(mu, sigma^2) depends on the data only through sum(x_i) and sum(x_i^2), because the exponent expands to -(1/(2 sigma^2))(sum x_i^2 - 2 mu sum x_i + n mu^2). So that pair is jointly sufficient for both parameters.", "id": "q3", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The maximum is sufficient for the upper endpoint of a Uniform(0, theta), not for a Gaussian's mean and variance.", "2": "The sample mean alone is sufficient only when sigma^2 is KNOWN; with sigma^2 unknown you also need sum(x_i^2).", "3": "The median is not sufficient: it discards information about the spread and about the exact values."}}, {"topic": "Woodbury", "text": "The Woodbury identity is most useful computationally when:", "options": ["U and V are square", "the low-rank update C⁻¹+VA⁻¹U is much smaller than A", "A is small and dense", "A is singular"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Woodbury rewrites (A + UCV)^-1 using A^-1 plus a correction built from the k x k capacitance matrix C^-1 + V A^-1 U. The saving is real only when that inner matrix is far smaller than A, turning one n x n inverse into one k x k inverse with k << n.", "id": "q11", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "If U and V are square (k = n) the inner inverse is the same size as A, so nothing is saved.", "2": "If A is small and dense you can simply invert A + UCV directly; the identity exists to avoid re-inverting a LARGE A.", "3": "Woodbury requires A^-1 to exist; a singular A is exactly the case the identity cannot handle."}}, {"topic": "Natural gradient", "text": "The natural gradient direction is:", "options": ["∇L", "F⁻¹∇L where F is the Fisher matrix", "∇L/‖∇L‖", "−∇²L ∇L"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The natural gradient is F^-1 grad L, where F is the Fisher information matrix. It is the steepest-descent direction when distance between parameters is measured by KL divergence rather than Euclidean distance, so it is invariant to reparameterization.", "id": "q11_d2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Plain grad L is the EUCLIDEAN steepest-descent direction and changes under reparameterization.", "2": "Normalizing the gradient only rescales it; it keeps the same (Euclidean) direction and is not a metric change.", "3": "Preconditioning by the Hessian gives Newton's method (and with a minus sign this expression is not even Newton's step, which is -H^-1 grad L)."}}, {"topic": "Pseudoinverse", "text": "The minimum-norm solution of x₁+x₂=2 (i.e. Ax=b with A=[1 1], b=2) via A⁺b is:", "options": ["[1,1]", "[2,0]", "[0,2]", "[2,2]"], "correct": 0, "explain": "A = [1 1] is 1x2 so A+ = Aᵀ(AAᵀ)^-1 = [1,1]ᵀ / 2. Then A+b = [1,1]ᵀ * 2/2 = [1,1]. numpy pinv([[1,1]]) @ [2] returns [1,1]. Of all points on x1+x2 = 2 this is the one nearest the origin (norm sqrt2 ≈ 1.414).", "id": "q2_d2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "[2,0] satisfies the equation but has norm 2 > sqrt2, so it is a solution but not the minimum-norm one.", "2": "[0,2] also satisfies the equation with norm 2; the pseudoinverse always returns the shortest solution, which is symmetric here.", "3": "[2,2] is not even a solution: 2 + 2 = 4, not 2."}}, {"topic": "SGD convergence", "text": "For a convex non-smooth objective, SGD with averaging achieves an expected suboptimality of order:", "options": ["O(1/T²)", "O(e^{−T})", "O(1/T)", "O(1/√T)"], "correct": 3, "explain": "For convex but non-smooth objectives, stochastic (sub)gradient descent with iterate averaging and step sizes ~ 1/sqrt(T) gives E[f(xbar_T) - f*] = O(1/sqrt T). Adding strong convexity improves this to O(1/T); smoothness plus acceleration is needed for anything faster.", "id": "q9_d2", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "O(1/T^2) is the accelerated rate for SMOOTH convex problems (Nesterov), not for non-smooth stochastic ones.", "1": "An exponential (linear) rate requires strong convexity AND smoothness with exact gradients; stochastic noise alone rules it out.", "2": "O(1/T) is what STRONG convexity buys; plain convexity without smoothness gives only O(1/sqrt T)."}}]}
